message.reasoning:
I need to decide whether to bid on Kentucky Avenue in the auction.

I have no red properties. Kentucky would not complete a monopoly for me.

The auction is at $220 with a $18 base rent. I am in jail with $1179 cash. Player 4 has Park Place and Boardwalk with two houses, which poses a rental threat.

Player 4 has only one house on Park Place and two on Boardwalk. Their cash is only $74, so they cannot build further. Player 3 owns all four railroads and has pink properties with two to three houses built. Player 3's cash is just $97.

Player 3's pink properties are dangerous. Virginia with three houses pays $500. States with three houses pays $450. St Charles with two houses pays $150. Player 3 has only $97 cash so cannot build more.

Player 1 owns orange properties with houses. Tennessee with three houses pays $550. St James with two houses pays $200. New York with two houses pays $220. Player 1 has only $15 cash.

Player 1 is broke, so the threat of landing on Kentucky is minimal. The property is priced at $220 with a $110 mortgage value. I need Pennsylvania Avenue to complete my greens, and I still lack Oriental, Vermont, Baltic, and Atlantic. Buying Kentucky would block Player 3 from forming a second color set if they acquire Indiana later, and it would prevent Player 1 from completing reds if they obtain Illinois.

Player 1 started the auction after landing on Kentucky but could not afford it with only $15. Player 3 has Illinois and may bid modestly for Kentucky as a step toward completing reds, though they lack Indiana. Cash preservation is critical because I must eventually exit jail into a hostile board.

Player 1 and Player 4 are unlikely to bid aggressively. Player 1 has only $15 cash and is heavily mortgaged, so a cheap bid would not outbid them. Player 4 has $74 but needs that cash to rebuild houses on Boardwalk and Park Place, so they will not spend it on Kentucky.

I have $1179 and could win the auction cheaply. The property sits well after jail and Chance, yet its base rent of $18 is weak without a monopoly.

Mortgaging Kentucky would free $110, but paying more than that locks cash I may need later. The real prize is Pennsylvania Avenue at $320 to complete my greens. A green monopoly is the win condition. Even a single house on each green costs $200. With three properties, that is $600 per house level. Pacific and North Carolina pay $900 with three houses, $1100 with four, and $1275 with a hotel.

I have already failed to roll doubles twice. The next turn I must pay $50 and leave jail. I cannot afford to spend cash on Kentucky now.

A $1 bid is worth considering. If no one else raises it, I would own Kentucky for nearly nothing and gain a mortgage value of $110. That is strictly positive expected value. A bidding war is possible, but I can drop out later. The real risk is leaving jail with too little cash to survive the next roll.

Player 3 could complete a red monopoly if they acquire Indiana, which would be dangerous. Player 1 is broke and cannot build on Kentucky. Player 4 would only use it as a rent nuisance. Blocking Player 3 from a cheap Kentucky bid is the most valuable outcome.

A modest opening bid is the right strategy. I must not spend so much that I cannot buy Pennsylvania Avenue or survive my jail exit. Total liquidity reaches roughly $1699 if I mortgage every property, but that would sacrifice the greens I am about to complete. I need a reserve of at least $320 for PA plus survival cash. I am now calculating what rent I might face when I finally leave jail.

The spaces immediately after Jail are St Charles, States, Virginia, the Pennsylvania RR, St James, Community Chest, Tennessee, New York, Free Parking, Kentucky, Chance, and Indiana. Only Indiana is mortgaged and unrentable.

The exit roll from jail is heavily weighted toward expensive spaces. Rolling 4, 5, or 8 lands on States, Virginia, or Tennessee for $450–$550. That is a 33 percent chance of a major rent hit. Player 3 owns Illinois and the B&O RR, so the board is dangerous after leaving jail.

I can afford to bid up to about $80–120 for Kentucky. Player 3 has only $97, so they cannot outbid me. I will drop out above that ceiling and let them overpay.

Player 3 could mortgage their four railroads to bid higher, but they would not mortgage them for a red property. Player 4 has only $74 and may make a small bid.

Player 4 cannot build on dark blue, so a cheap Kentucky bid would give them rent. Player 1 can only bid $15. I should win the auction for under $100, perhaps under $50. Buying it for less than its $110 mortgage value gives me free optionality.

The $18 rent is too small to justify tying up cash. I am now checking whether mortgaging during an auction settlement or another player's turn is allowed.

Mortgaging during an auction is likely allowed when cash is needed. A bid up to the $110 mortgage value is safe because I can always mortgage back if I need the cash later. The downside is a 10 percent interest rate and lost rent while mortgaged. I will open with a modest bid rather than $1 so I do not look weak and so the auction may end quickly.

A $1 opening bid would reveal interest without committing cash. A higher bid might scare off the cash-poor opponents. I will open with $25 or $30. That signals intent while staying safely below the $110 mortgage value.

I will bid $1. That is the information-maximizing move. If no one else raises it, I win for almost nothing. If they outbid me, I can reassess on my next turn.

I will keep my bidding ceiling private and avoid sounding eager for the property. The hard limit is roughly $100–$110, but I prefer to win under $50. Blocking Player 3 from a cheap red is only a minor strategic benefit, not a monopoly-completing move. I must not drain cash before leaving jail.

A bid of $16 would eliminate Player 1, who only has $15. Player 1 cannot mortgage properties with houses, so they would need to sell a house on an orange property to raise cash. Selling one house returns only $50, which is not enough to outbid me.

A $16 bid would eliminate Player 1, who only has $15 and cannot mortgage houses to raise cash. That leaves only Player 3, whose $97 is too low to outbid me without mortgaging. A $75 bid would instead remove Player 4 and pressure Player 3.

A $75 bid is the chosen opening. It is safely below the $110 mortgage value, so I would gain at least $35 in equity plus rent upside and block Player 3 from a cheap red. After paying the $50 jail fee, I would still have roughly $1054, which survives a worst-case exit hit of $550 and leaves enough cash to buy Pennsylvania Avenue. This avoids a bidding war while still winning cheaply.

A $1 opening bid risks a bidding war that could push the price to $40–60. A $75 opener would end the auction cleanly but overpay by $25–50. The property is worth roughly $80–120 to me, yet my opponents value it far less because they need cash more desperately.

Player 3 values a red near Illinois at $40–80, and Player 4 at $20–40. A $21 opening bid would eliminate Player 1 while keeping the price modest. Still, a $1 bid is the dominant probe. A dismissive message with that low bid might make opponents think I will drop out quickly, which could backfire if they raise to $2 and I respond.

A $1 opening bid is the right choice. It avoids setting a high anchor, and other AIs will bid because the property is still positive expected value at that price. I will keep my public message short and dismissive, perhaps saying "I'll start it at a dollar." My private ceiling remains around $100, but I prefer to win under $50 so I can still afford Pennsylvania Avenue and survive a worst-case jail exit.

The auction is on Player 1's turn, so I will exit jail immediately after it ends. I will not mortgage Ventnor, Connecticut, or the greens.

Their pink properties are already built and generating rent, so this hurts their ability to pay upcoming orange and pink hits.

I have served two jail turns. The next turn I must roll doubles or pay $50 to exit. Turn 92 is p1's auction turn, not mine.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. ### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.
